title: Experience Doesn't Always Translate Into Expertise
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article questions the common leadership assumption that years of experience reliably signal expertise. Drawing on research into physicians and race car drivers, it shows that experience only builds mastery when it includes variety, feedback, and deliberate reflection; repeating the same routine tasks for years can produce stagnation rather than growth. The piece urges leaders to interrogate the substance of a person's experience during hiring and promotion decisions, rather than treating tenure itself as a proxy for skill. Its core reframe is memorable: the real question isn't how many years of experience someone has, but whether it was genuinely varied learning or the same two weeks repeated many times over.
points: Experience is widely treated as a proxy for expertise in hiring, promotion, and pay decisions.
Research shows experience is only a weak-to-average predictor of expertise, depending heavily on its quality.
Physicians with the greatest mastery were those exposed to varied, complex cases rather than routine repetition.
Race car drivers with fewer years of experience often out-perform tenured peers due to deliberate practice and feedback.
Leaders should scrutinize what challenges, feedback, and variety a person's experience actually included.
quotes: Despite this common wisdom and practice, research has shown that experience is an imperfect proxy for expertise.
Their understanding, knowledge, and expertise plateau early in their tenure because their experience is routine.
The physicians with the greatest mastery were those who saw a high variety of cases and learned to adapt their behavior to changing contexts.
Studies confirm that deliberate training, feedback, and continuous refinement are much stronger predictors of expertise for drivers.
Is it 20 years of experience, or two weeks of experience over 20 years?
